Qualitative structure of a discrete-time Markov chain

Source: R/chain_structure.R
chain_structure.Rd

chain_structure() describes the qualitative structure of a discrete-time Markov chain: the properties that depend only on which transitions are possible (the support of the transition matrix), not on any starting distribution. It classifies every state as absorbing, recurrent or transient, finds the communicating classes and the period of each recurrent state, says whether the chain is irreducible, aperiodic, regular and reversible, and computes the hitting probabilities and, when transient states exist, the probability that each ends in each closed class (an absorbing state or a closed class of several states) and the expected number of steps it takes to enter one. It reads a transition network, a tna model, a transition matrix or sequences, and analyses a grouped network one network at a time.

It is a diagnostic to run before trusting passage_time() or markov_stability(). Both assume a regular chain (irreducible and aperiodic), whose stationary distribution is unique; is_regular says whether that holds. The structure follows the estimated matrix: a transition never observed in the data counts as impossible, so a chain estimated from few sequences can look reducible because a rare move was not seen.

Usage

chain_structure(x, normalize = TRUE, tol = 1e-10)

# S3 method for class 'chain_structure'
print(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'chain_structure'
plot(x, show_values = TRUE, digits = 2L, ...)

# S3 method for class 'chain_structure'
summary(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'chain_structure_group'
print(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'chain_structure_group'
summary(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'summary_chain_structure'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

x

The chain: a netobject, bare cograph_network or tna model with transition weights, a numeric transition matrix, or a wide sequence data frame or character matrix (estimated with build_network(method = "relative")). A netobject_group is analysed network by network. An association network (cor, pcor, glasso, ising, mgm) or a matrix with negative entries raises an error of class nestimate_not_markov. For the print() and plot() methods: a chain_structure object (print() also takes a chain_structure_group or a summary_chain_structure).

normalize

Whether to rescale rows that do not sum to 1 so that they do, with a warning, as passage_time() does. Default TRUE. With FALSE, such a matrix raises an error. A state with no outgoing transitions (a row of zeros) raises an error either way.

tol

The tolerance below which a transition probability counts as zero when the support graph is built (it drives classification, communicating_classes, period and hitting_probabilities), and the tolerance of the reversibility check (detailed balance). Default 1e-10. It does not govern the absorbing-state test: a state is absorbing only when P[i, i] equals 1 to a fixed internal tolerance of .Machine$double.eps^0.5, so raising tol to ignore tiny transition probabilities never reclassifies a near-deterministic state as absorbing.

...

Ignored, except by the print() methods of a chain_structure_group, which pass it to each network's print(), and of a summary_chain_structure, which pass it to print.data.frame().

show_values

For the plot() method: whether to print each cell's probability inside it. Default TRUE. Values are never printed for more than 20 states; set FALSE earlier when the labels overlap (from about 10 states).

digits

For the plot() method: decimal places of the cell values. Default 2.

object

For the summary() methods: a chain_structure or chain_structure_group object.

Value

A chain_structure object, or for a netobject_group a chain_structure_group (class c("chain_structure_group", "list")), a named list holding one chain_structure per network. print() shows the chain-level properties (for a group, one block per network); summary() returns a data frame (see Summary columns): for a chain_structure, one row per state, of class c("summary_chain_structure", "data.frame"), carrying the chain-level flags is_regular, is_irreducible, is_aperiodic, is_reversible, n_classes and absorbing_states as attributes that its print() method shows as a header above the table; for a chain_structure_group, a plain data frame with one row per group and state. plot() returns a ggplot heatmap of the hitting probabilities (see Plot colours). The print() methods return their input invisibly.

The fields of a chain_structure:

states

Character vector of state names.

classification

Named character vector, one of "absorbing", "recurrent" or "transient" per state.

communicating_classes

List of state-name vectors, one per strongly connected component of the support graph.

recurrent_classes

The communicating classes that are closed (no transition leaves the class).

transient_classes

The communicating classes that are not closed.

absorbing_states

Character vector of states with P[i, i] = 1, tested to within .Machine$double.eps^0.5; tol does not relax this.

period

Named integer vector: the period of each recurrent state, NA for transient states.

is_irreducible

TRUE when there is exactly one communicating class.

is_aperiodic

TRUE when every recurrent state has period 1.

is_regular

is_irreducible && is_aperiodic.

is_reversible

TRUE when the chain satisfies detailed balance against its stationary distribution; NA for a chain that is not irreducible (no unique stationary distribution).

hitting_probabilities

n x n matrix whose [i, j] entry is the probability of ever reaching j from i, computed over the same tol-thresholded support graph as classification, so the two agree: a state in a closed class has hitting probability 0 to every state outside it.

absorption_probabilities

n_transient x n_closed matrix whose [i, j] entry is the probability that the chain started in transient state i ends in closed class j; each row sums to 1. An absorbing state is a column named after it; a closed class of several states is one column named by its states joined with + (for example B+C). NULL when the chain has no transient state.

mean_absorption_time

Named numeric vector of the expected number of steps each transient state takes to enter a closed class, whichever it is. NULL when absorption_probabilities is.

P

The transition matrix analysed (after any row normalisation).

Details

The fundamental-matrix absorption analysis follows Kemeny & Snell (1976), with every closed class lumped into one absorbing state, so each transient state's absorption probabilities sum to 1; the hitting probabilities are the minimal non-negative solution of the linear system in Norris (1997), solved over the states that can reach the target. The diagonal of the hitting matrix uses the return-time convention, the probability of returning to the state in one or more steps, as markovchain::hittingProbabilities() does.

Plot colours

The plot() method draws the hitting-probability matrix as a heatmap, with rows and columns ordered by communicating class (closed classes first, larger classes before smaller ones) so the block structure is visible. Cell colour runs from white (0) to dark blue (1) and encodes P(ever reach j | start at i); the diagonal uses the return-time convention, P(return to j in >= 1 steps). The state labels on both axes name each state's class, as in Active (recurrent), and the subtitle lists the chain-level properties. A chain that is not irreducible shows zero entries between classes that cannot reach each other; when every state ends in one absorbing state, that state's column is all 1s.

Summary columns

summary() of a chain_structure returns one row per state, combining every per-state result: state, classification, period, persistence (the diagonal of the transition matrix), return_probability (the diagonal of the hitting matrix) and sojourn_steps (1 / (1 - persistence), Inf for an absorbing state). An irreducible chain adds stationary_probability. A chain with transient states adds absorption_probability (one closed class) or one absorbed_in_<class> column per closed class (named as the columns of absorption_probabilities), and mean_absorption_time (steps to enter a closed class); these are NA for states that are not transient. Probabilities are rounded to 4 decimals and step counts to 2. Columns are ordered for readability: identifiers first, classification second, per-state results last.

summary() of a chain_structure_group stacks these tables into one data frame with a group column first, one row per group and state; a column that only some groups have is NA for the others.

References

Kemeny, J. G. and Snell, J. L. (1976). Finite Markov Chains. Springer-Verlag.

Norris, J. R. (1997). Markov Chains. Cambridge University Press.

See also

passage_time(), markov_stability(), build_network()

Examples

net <- build_network(as.data.frame(trajectories), method = "relative")
cs  <- chain_structure(net)
print(cs)
#> Chain structure  [3 states, 1 communicating classes]
#>   irreducible: TRUE   aperiodic: TRUE   regular: TRUE   reversible: FALSE
#>   recurrent classes: 1   transient classes: 0
#> 
#> Use summary(x) for the per-state table, plot(x) for the heatmap.
# \donttest{
summary(cs)
#> Chain structure summary  [3 states, 1 classes]
#>   irreducible: TRUE   aperiodic: TRUE   regular: TRUE   reversible: FALSE
#> 
#>       state classification period persistence return_probability sojourn_steps
#>      Active      recurrent      1      0.6976                  1          3.31
#>     Average      recurrent      1      0.6099                  1          2.56
#>  Disengaged      recurrent      1      0.4831                  1          1.93
#>  stationary_probability
#>                  0.3719
#>                  0.4431
#>                  0.1850
# }
